scenes.title: The broken status quo
scenes.narration: If you have ever waited with a parent for a hospital bed, you know the quiet despair of a long, silent queue. The bed crunch is not only a shortage of rooms. It is a failure to orchestrate the beds a hospital already has.

scenes.title: Today, without the system
scenes.narration: When public broadcasters documented this crisis, they confirmed what leaders already knew. You cannot build your way out of a flow bottleneck. Phone tag between departments, cubicles frozen by cohort locks, and afternoon discharge gridlock all conspire to hide capacity.

scenes.title: Before and after: the ED handoff
scenes.narration: Take the very first step. Today an attending pages a registrar and waits, notes are written on paper and re-keyed. We wanted the opposite: findings synthesised on arrival, confirmed in one click, and sent onward with no phone call at all.

scenes.title: ED intake queue
scenes.narration: In the Emergency Department, every waiting patient is ranked and ready to review. Our first patient, Chua Wee Kiat, presents with acute coronary syndrome, a troponin of one hundred and eighty, and a falling blood pressure.

scenes.title: Opening the smart dossier
scenes.narration: Opening his dossier, the system has already done the reading.

scenes.title: Pre-populated directives
scenes.narration: It proposes an acuity tier, the cardiology service, a class B two bed, continuous telemetry, and fall precautions. The attending reviews, rather than retypes, and confirms the admission directly.

scenes.title: The five-tier framework
scenes.narration: The same dossier covers the whole disposition spectrum, from tier one critical to tier five short-stay observation. A stable patient with a normal troponin would instead default to general medicine, with no telemetry required.

scenes.title: Specialist broadcast pool
scenes.narration: Complex cases go to a specialist broadcast pool, not a phone queue. Consults for many clusters run in parallel, each with its own service level countdown, so no request is ever lost to an unmonitored feed.

scenes.title: Safety-first discordance
scenes.narration: A second opinion is where safety is won or lost. Here the emergency tier read acute stable, but the cardiologist sees a rising troponin and dynamic changes, and upgrades to tier two with mandatory telemetry.

scenes.title: Chained consult
scenes.narration: His case also spawns a concurrent surgery review for concurrent abdominal pain. Multi-specialty cases run in parallel, and the consensus gate stays open until every consult resolves, rather than waiting in a serial queue of phone calls.

scenes.title: Direct digital bed queue
scenes.narration: The moment consensus is reached, a structured packet lands in the bed management queue. No calls were placed. The coordinator sees admissions ranked by acuity, with the higher, safer tier already adopted.

scenes.title: Reconcile without blocking
scenes.narration: Autonomy is preserved. For any admission, the coordinator can open a side-by-side comparison of the emergency assessment and the specialist consults, and prompt a clinical reconciliation, while the safer tentative bed assignment continues without blocking.

steps.name: View Comparative Notes
steps.target: View Comparative Notes button on a queue row

scenes.title: Before and after: diversion
scenes.narration: Not every admission needs a scarce acute bed. But diversion used to carry a paperwork tax so heavy that clinicians defaulted to acute beds anyway.

scenes.title: MIC at Home diversion
scenes.narration: Mrs Tan Boon Hwa is clinically stable enough for hospital-level care at home. The system has diverted her to a mobile inpatient care virtual ward, and her tracker explains the alternative step-down pathway, freeing a physical bed while she is monitored daily.

scenes.title: Sister community hospital
scenes.narration: Mr Ahmad Ibrahim, recovering from a stroke, is referred to Outram Community Hospital for step-down rehabilitation. The digital packet dispatches with a thirty-minute bilateral service level timer, no phone negotiation required.

scenes.title: Financial and care explainer
scenes.narration: The family sees a plain-language explainer: ward-class co-pay bands, means-tested subsidy, and direct lines to a medical social worker and financial counselling. Peace of mind, with no deposits and no signatures.

scenes.title: Ghost capacity
scenes.narration: But a queue is only as good as the beds behind it. And many beds sit empty on paper, yet locked in practice. A single patient can freeze an entire six-bed cubicle.

scenes.title: The four-state bed lifecycle
scenes.narration: Every bed moves through a strict four-state lifecycle: mustard yellow while cleaning, white when clean and available, green once assigned and in transit, and grey when occupied. The live inventory matrix shows all of it at a glance.

scenes.title: Constraint solver recommendations
scenes.narration: Tan Ah Meng needs a telemetry bed with fall precautions. A pure-Java heuristic scores every candidate against four hard safety invariants and three soft rules, and returns the top three beds with the reasoning made explicit.

steps.target: Select button on the Tan Ah Meng admission row

scenes.title: Pack first, then batch
scenes.narration: The insight that recovers ghost capacity is the ordering. First the solver packs waiting patients into partly filled cubicles that already match their cohort. Only then does it designate a whole clean cubicle for a surge cluster.

scenes.title: Batch holding ward
scenes.narration: When three male patients of the same class and infection profile wait together, the system detects the surge and recommends a single flexible holding ward for the whole cohort, in one click.

scenes.title: Dynamic cohort-swap
scenes.narration: One patient, David Koh, blocks a flexible ward while still in the Emergency Department. The solver proposes moving him to an equivalent bed elsewhere. A single approval, guarded against concurrent edits, liberates the whole room.

scenes.title: Tunable solver policy
scenes.narration: The scoring behind those matches is not a black box. Coordinators tune specialty alignment, cubicle packing, and fall-risk proximity, or switch whole presets when a surge demands it.

scenes.title: Patient milestone tracker
scenes.narration: The family sees the same journey, without the anxiety. A phone link shows three clear milestones, the estimated wait, and the queue position within their own ward class. No calls to the nurses' counter.

scenes.title: Empathetic delay tag
scenes.narration: And when a wait is unavoidable, the tone changes. Madam Wong's isolation room is finishing a mandatory disinfection cycle, and the tracker explains why, in plain, reassuring language, with a hotline to call.

scenes.title: Before and after: discharge
scenes.narration: That leaves the last bottleneck, and the most stubborn one: getting patients out. The afternoon discharge gridlock traps beds that ED patients are waiting for in the hallway.

scenes.title: Discharge runway
scenes.narration: On the ward, discharge starts two to three days early. Each occupied bed carries an estimated discharge date and a clinical confidence, so nurses can engage caregivers well before the morning of departure.

scenes.title: Sign-off queues bedside meds
scenes.narration: A morning sign-off does two things at once. It clears the patient to leave, and it automatically queues the discharge medicines to be packed and delivered to the bedside before eleven, retiring the human bottleneck days early.

scenes.title: Thirty-minute turnover, closed loop
scenes.narration: The instant a bed is vacated it turns mustard yellow, and a thirty-minute cleaning clock begins. When housekeeping signs off, the bed doesn't just turn white; it automatically notifies bed management that it is allocatable again.

scenes.title: Every decision measured
scenes.narration: Every step you have seen leaves a measurable trace. The control tower is proof that the system is instrumented and audit-ready, with each metric extractable through two independent pathways.

scenes.title: Control tower: intake
scenes.narration: Here is the live dashboard. Twenty-one bed requests, every one of them digital and phone-free. Specialist claim latency under a minute. And a concordance rate that shows the safety mechanism resolving genuine disagreement.

scenes.title: Control tower: allocation
scenes.narration: On the allocation side: two diversions preserving acute beds, one to a community hospital and one to hospital-at-home. A batch holding ward adoption rate that measures the pack-then-batch strategy at work.

scenes.title: Control tower: experience and discharge
scenes.narration: And across experience and discharge: prolonged-wait communication and periodic updates at full coverage, bedside medication delivery, and a housekeeping turnover averaging twenty-six minutes, comfortably inside the thirty-minute target.

scenes.title: Call to action
scenes.narration: Bed capacity is not fixed. When decisions are synthesised in real time, constraints are solved by mathematics rather than by phone, and discharge is pulled into the morning, we recover the capacity that was there all along. Explore the live prototype.
